role_en: Hold cities, magazines and fortresses until the field army arrives.
lore_en: The least celebrated arm of the Castilian war machine is often the first to fight. Plaza companies guard arsenals, railheads, harbour gates and frontier towns with older but serviceable weapons. Their task is not glory; it is to keep a city functioning long enough for the Tercio to answer. Arc IV reform begins to standardise their stores and reporting, turning scattered garrisons into a reliable first layer of defence.
quote_en: “The wall before the army.”

role_en: Hold the line, manoeuvre by small units and keep fighting after command disruption.
lore_en: The Fusileros are the clearest face of the 1717 reform. Their Spencer Modelo 1716 muskets, ammunition pouches, medical kit and communications equipment are issued to common standards. More important than the weapon is the habit behind it: junior leaders are expected to act when orders fail, and a unit is trained to survive the loss of its officer rather than freeze around the empty space.
quote_en: “The line must survive the officer.”

role_en: Break defended streets, trenches, gates and breaches at close range.
lore_en: Grenadier companies are drawn from soldiers trusted to keep moving when the battlefield becomes too cramped for elegant drill. They carry grenades, short firearms and heavy bayonets or sabres, and are commonly attached to formations preparing an assault on a breach or urban strongpoint. Their purpose is brutally simple: create room for the rest of the Tercio to enter, then hold that room long enough for the line to reform behind them.
quote_en: “Open the breach. We will make it wider.”

role_en: Remove officers, artillery crews and exposed Vestigium components before the line closes.
lore_en: Tiradores are selected for judgement as much as marksmanship. They operate ahead of the main body, hunting command figures, signalling teams and the vulnerable mechanisms that allow enemy artillery or Vestigium systems to function. Castilian doctrine does not ask them to win a battle alone. Their work is to make the enemy formation just a little blinder, slower and less certain before the Tercio reaches effective range.
quote_en: “One shot, one problem less.”

role_en: Stop cavalry, undead rushes and large Vestigium creatures before they reach the gun line.
lore_en: The pike survived in Castilian service because the world kept producing things that a bayonet line could not safely stop. Reformed Piqueros use shorter, stronger polearms than their sixteenth-century predecessors and train beside firearms rather than apart from them. They are deployed where momentum itself is the threat: cavalry lanes, breaches, narrow streets and the expected path of a creature too large to be trusted to musket fire alone.
quote_en: “Some problems still require a wall of steel.”

role_en: Build the road, bridge, breach or fieldwork that the battle requires.
lore_en: Royal Sappers are the quiet reason many Castilian plans remain possible after the map stops matching the ground. They bridge streams, cut roads, raise obstacles, repair damaged gun positions and place demolition charges under fire. Arc IV reform pushes their methods into standard manuals so a bridge can still be completed after the officer who designed it is removed from the exercise. Their ideal victory is a battlefield where everyone else forgets how much work made it usable.
quote_en: “If the road does not exist, make one.”

role_en: Enter places ordinary infantry is not expected to survive and force an outcome.
lore_en: Conquistadores are not merely better Fusileros. They are expeditionary assault troops chosen for boarding, breach fighting, hostile ruins and encounters where ordinary formations cannot maintain their preferred distance. Their equipment varies by mission, but heavy close-combat weapons, short firearms and protective gear are common. They are expensive to train and intentionally scarce. When a commander asks for Conquistadores, the battlefield has already become abnormal.
quote_en: “Send the Tercio to hold it. Send us to enter it.”

role_en: Seize crossings, reinforce threatened sectors and fight dismounted where cavalry cannot.
lore_en: Royal Dragoons use the horse as a weapon of time rather than prestige. They ride hard to the point that matters, dismount, and fight with carbines or shortened Modelo firearms while their mounts are held under cover. This makes them especially useful across Iberia and North Africa, where a road junction or bridge may matter more than a glorious charge. They are often the first regular troops to arrive and the last to remain mobile.
quote_en: “Arrive as cavalry. Fight as infantry.”

role_en: Counter-charge, exploit a broken line and strike artillery or exposed flanks.
lore_en: The Andalusian horse retains the visual memory of an older Castilian military culture, but its place in the modern army is carefully defined. These riders are held as a mobile reserve until infantry and artillery have created the opening they need. Lance, sabre and pistol remain their tools; patience is the discipline Arc IV demands from them. A failed charge is expensive. A charge delivered into a formation already bending can end a battle.
quote_en: “The charge is the answer, not the question.”

role_en: Move with the army and place reliable fire where infantry needs it most.
lore_en: The ordinary light battery lacks the spectacle of Castilia’s experimental guns, yet it remains the artillery arm commanders trust every day. Its pieces can be limbered quickly, supplied through established ammunition routes and shifted when a firing angle becomes unsafe or useless. In North Africa these batteries travel with infantry columns and fortified supply points alike. Their virtue is not novelty but the ability to appear, fire, move and be supplied again.
quote_en: “The gun that arrives is worth more than the gun left behind.”

role_en: Suppress infantry and hold breaches with sequential four-barrel fire.
lore_en: The Royal Organ of Four Voices is the most mature of Castilia’s new multi-barrel pieces. Four breech-loading barrels fire in sequence while the first is already being opened and reloaded. More important is its redundancy: a damaged barrel can be isolated without silencing the entire platform. It is still demanding in ammunition and crew training, but unlike a laboratory curiosity it has begun to resemble a weapon that a field army can genuinely maintain.
quote_en: “Four voices. One answer.”

role_en: Flood choke points and fortified approaches with sustained fire.
lore_en: Tempestad sacrifices mobility for density of fire. Six breech-loading barrels sit on a chained firing frame fed by trays of ammunition and hand-worked mechanisms. Once anchored, it can maintain a punishing rhythm that makes narrow approaches almost uninhabitable. The price is obvious: soft ground, rapid retreats and long supply lines are its enemies. Castilian command therefore treats Tempestad as a fortress weapon, not a trophy to drag into every campaign.
quote_en: “Do not bring the storm where the road cannot feed it.”

role_en: Deliver immense electrical discharge from a surveyed and prepared firing site.
lore_en: Fulminante is less a cannon than a temporary electrical installation built around a weapon. Steel anchors, insulated coils, modular accumulators and a steam generator must be assembled before the system can safely concentrate its discharge. A good site may take hours to prepare. The result is extraordinary, but Arc IV doctrine refuses to confuse extraordinary power with field usefulness. Weather, terrain and retreat planning are considered part of the weapon itself.
quote_en: “Power begins with choosing the ground.”

role_en: Identify, contain and destroy Vestigium threats without relying on a unique hero or relic.
lore_en: These mixed teams embody the deepest purpose of the Arc IV reform. Reliquiario knowledge is paired with Conquistador field discipline, but their standard teams are deliberately equipped with tools Castilia can reproduce: detectors, containment gear, specialised ammunition and documented procedures. They do not carry a miracle for every problem. Their value is that another team can be trained, supplied and sent after them if the first does not return.
quote_en: “Understand it before you decide how to kill it.”

class_en: Crown Exceptional Order · One Hundred Numbers
role_en: Act as strategic assets, protect the Crown and confront threats beyond normal formations.
lore_en: The Royal Guard is an order of one hundred numbered individuals, not a regiment. Each member may carry a distinct Vestigium, combat doctrine or political duty, so Uno, IV, VII, VIII and XII are never interchangeable assets. Castilia can deploy them but cannot reproduce them. Arc IV reform therefore treats the Guard as strategic force multipliers while rebuilding the ordinary army to survive whenever these exceptional people are absent.
quote_en: “A hundred people were never meant to be a wall.”

role_en: Break enemy fleet formations with armour, high battle speed and turret fire that remains effective through rapid manoeuvre.
lore_en: Only seven hulls of this generation exist. Each combines three masts, four boilers, steel armour and heavy rotating turrets fore and aft, allowing cruise under sail and reduced steam before surging to roughly fifteen knots in battle. Eight broadside guns remain on each side, but Edward’s doctrine rarely uses them: the ship is built to cross, split and out-turn a line while the turrets keep firing.
quote_en: “A line exists only until one of these ships crosses it.”

role_en: Anchor choke points and fleet bases with armour and firepower too heavy for ordinary sailing warships to dislodge.
lore_en: Castilia’s first ironclads were conceived as moving fortresses rather than true ocean-going battleships. Massive boiler machinery, reinforced internal structure and heavy protection make them brutally resilient, but fuel consumption and limited cruising endurance punish long deployments. Around Gibraltar they remain terrifying defensive assets; sent too far from prepared support, their own weight becomes the enemy.
quote_en: “Too heavy to chase. Too hard to remove.”

role_en: Screen the battle fleet, hunt raiders and escort valuable formations without committing a battleship to every threat.
lore_en: The armoured frigate protects machinery, magazines and vital gun positions rather than wrapping the entire hull in battleship-weight steel. Full sailing rig gives economical range, while auxiliary steam provides the burst of speed needed to intercept raiders or hold station with modern capital ships. It trades heavy-gun endurance for the ability to be almost everywhere the main fleet needs a hard escort.
quote_en: “Fast enough to find the battle. Armoured enough to return from it.”

role_en: Pursue light warships through confined coastal waters where heavier Castilian hulls lose manoeuvring freedom.
lore_en: Armoured corvettes combine shallow draft, compact steam machinery and selective protection around their fighting core. They are designed for the ugly waters close to ports, shoals and headlands, where xebecs, galleys and raiders try to escape a fleet built around larger ships. Their guns are modest by Castilian standards, but their ability to keep speed when the wind fails makes them dangerous hunters.
quote_en: “Where the battleship cannot follow, the corvette finishes the chase.”

role_en: Patrol distant sea lanes, protect commerce and scout independently without consuming battleship resources.
lore_en: The steam-sail cruiser is built around range rather than maximum protection. Sail carries it across long patrols with minimal fuel demand; steam is reserved for battle, interception and escape. It can escort convoys, hunt commerce raiders and maintain contact far ahead of the main fleet, giving Castilian admirals modern operational reach without spending an ironclad on routine patrol.
quote_en: “Coal for battle. Wind for the journey.”

class_en: Royal Ship of the Line · Heavy Broadside
role_en: Hold the conventional battle line and deliver sustained broadside fire behind the fleet’s faster specialised ships.
lore_en: The Royal ship of the line remains the numerical backbone of Castilian blue-water warfare. Its hull is heavily braced, ammunition standards are shared across the Crown fleet and gun crews drill to maintain fire even after rigging or officers are lost. Modern ironclads have not made these ships obsolete; they have simply narrowed the battles they are expected to fight.
quote_en: “Old wood. Modern discipline.”

role_en: Hold a fixed sector with enormous wooden broadside weight and punish any formation forced into its firing arc.
lore_en: The four-deck warships fielded by the Andalusian councils are slow, immense and unapologetically traditional. Their value lies in the sheer density of guns carried behind a reinforced wooden hull, making each vessel a mobile wall when positioned correctly. They do not chase fast enemies; they make parts of the sea too expensive to enter.
quote_en: “It does not pursue. It waits for you to enter range.”

role_en: Scout, screen the fleet, chase damaged ships and strike logistics before heavier formations commit.
lore_en: Royal frigates perform the work that keeps Castilian capital ships from wasting their strength. They range ahead for reconnaissance, guard open flanks, relay signals, pursue crippled enemies and attack exposed supply vessels. At Melilla, frigates repeatedly entered waters the heavy line would not, proving that seeing the battle first is often more useful than carrying another deck of guns.
quote_en: “The fleet sees because the frigates are already there.”

role_en: Carry signals, officers and reconnaissance reports faster than the battle line can reposition.
lore_en: The fleet cutter is small enough to be dismissed until an admiral needs information moved immediately. Its shallow draft and generous sail plan let it work coastlines, carry pilots, relay orders and maintain contact between formations separated by smoke or weather. It has little reason to remain in a serious gun duel; its weapon is keeping the fleet informed and connected.
quote_en: “A fleet that cannot speak is already half defeated.”

role_en: Provide the stable firing line around which the Caliphate’s more mobile arms can manoeuvre.
lore_en: Makhzen Fusiliers are the conventional face of the Moorish army: salaried regulars, properly supplied and trained to hold ground that skirmishers and cavalry cannot. They are not intended to outshoot a reformed Castilian Tercio in a prolonged duel. Their value is steadiness. A column can raid, disperse and wheel around the battlefield because somewhere behind it stands a body of infantry that will still be there when the movement ends.
quote_en: “Someone must still be there when the dust clears.”

role_en: Dominate ridgelines, passes and broken ground with long-range selective fire.
lore_en: Rif riflemen are recruited from communities where distance, wind and stone have always mattered more than parade-ground geometry. Their long guns are slow to handle in a close fight but dangerous from slopes that conceal both shooter and retreat. They favour officers, gun crews and exposed messengers, then change position before the answer arrives. Against them, the battlefield often feels empty until someone important falls.
quote_en: “If you can see the ridge, the ridge can see you.”

role_en: Harass, ambush and seize ground that formed infantry cannot use efficiently.
lore_en: Atlas Skirmishers travel light and treat difficult ground as cover rather than obstacle. They move through gullies, broken villages and mountain paths in small groups, firing from angles that make a conventional response awkward. Their task is rarely to hold the centre. Instead they bleed the edges of a formation, force guards onto unwanted routes and keep the enemy looking sideways while the main Moorish body chooses where to commit.
quote_en: “The mountain does not need a formation.”

role_en: Guard wells, caravan routes and isolated posts beyond easy reinforcement.
lore_en: Frontier companies are shaped by distance. Their uniforms and weapons are less uniform than those of the Makhzen, but their officers understand the practical arithmetic of the desert: water, shade, ammunition, animal condition and the number of days before help can arrive. They patrol wells and caravan routes, escort survey teams and hold lonely posts where a battle may begin with silence rather than gunfire.
quote_en: “Count the water before you count the enemy.”

role_en: Hold the point the Sultan or Caliph cannot afford to lose.
lore_en: The Caliphal Guard is the Moorish answer to the need for a formation that can simply stand and fight. Better armed and more consistently equipped than provincial units, it protects the ruler, key headquarters and the final reserve of a field army. Unlike the Hashashin, its prestige is visible and deliberate. When the Guard enters the line, the message is not subtlety but commitment: the state has decided this ground matters.
quote_en: “Where the banner remains, the state remains.”

role_en: Create unexpectedly dense musket fire from a tiny, highly mobile firing station.
lore_en: Camel Gunners are one of the Caliphate’s most distinctive battlefield systems. The animal kneels, the firing rest is set, and a small crew turns several loaded guns through one shooter’s hands while another man reloads. The result is a rhythm of fire out of proportion to the number of men visible. When pressure builds, the rest folds, the camel rises and the entire firing point moves before enemy artillery can settle onto it.
quote_en: “Three men, six guns, one cloud of dust.”

role_en: See farther, travel longer and return with information instead of trophies.
lore_en: Camel Scouts are not assault cavalry. Their value is measured in routes mapped, wells confirmed, tracks read and columns found before those columns realise they have been observed. A good scout patrol can remain detached for days, living lightly enough to avoid the logistical wake that betrays larger forces. In the Sahara, this makes them one of the Caliphate’s most strategically valuable units despite their modest battlefield presence.
quote_en: “The report is the victory.”

role_en: Exploit exposed flanks, broken formations and retreating artillery.
lore_en: Guich Lancers preserve the Caliphate’s mounted striking power without pretending to be armoured European knights. They rely on speed, local horsemanship and the discipline to wait until the enemy is already occupied. Their best charge lands after rifle fire, rough ground or another unit has broken the target’s order. A Guich commander who attacks too early wastes horses; one who arrives at the right moment turns disorder into collapse.
quote_en: “Strike the formation after it forgets its shape.”

role_en: Harass columns, screen flanks and pull slower enemies out of position.
lore_en: Horse Carbiniers blur the line between cavalry and skirmisher. They fire from the saddle or after a rapid dismount, then move before the enemy can turn a full formation toward them. They are particularly effective against marching columns and artillery escorts, where a few minutes of confusion matter more than casualties. Their purpose is irritation made operational: to force a commander to waste time, ammunition and attention.
quote_en: “Make them turn. Then make them turn again.”

role_en: Fire, displace and fire again before counter-battery fire can settle.
lore_en: Moorish field artillery favours pieces that can survive the army’s tempo. Calibre is sacrificed when necessary for easier movement, faster limbering and compatibility with roads that are barely roads at all. Batteries are expected to change angle often, support cavalry and infantry in short bursts and leave before a heavier enemy gun line completes its response. Mobility is not an accessory to their firepower; it is the reason the guns stay alive.
quote_en: “A gun that stays too long becomes a landmark.”

role_en: Bring artillery into passes, ridges and narrow routes inaccessible to normal gun teams.
lore_en: Mountain guns are deliberately small enough to be broken down and carried by pack animals. Their shells cannot compete with the weight of a fortress piece, but that comparison misses the point. A light gun on a ridge where the enemy expected no gun at all can dominate a road, a village entrance or a climbing column. Moor commanders use them to turn difficult terrain from a limitation into a firing platform.
quote_en: “The impossible gun position is often the best one.”

role_en: Scout, sabotage, mark targets, recover people and disturb enemy command without being fixed in battle.
lore_en: Hashashin are feared most when nobody can prove they were present. They move through cities, camps and broken front lines with minimal identifying marks, passing information through quiet networks rather than dramatic displays. Their work includes reconnaissance, sabotage, extraction and the selective removal of a problem that cannot be solved openly. They are not line assassins meant to duel whole formations. If a Hashashin unit is fighting like ordinary infantry, something has already gone wrong.
quote_en: “The enemy should notice the result before the hand.”

role_en: Keep water, ammunition, medicine and spare animals moving through a dispersed army.
lore_en: The Caravan Corps is the formation outsiders underestimate until their own army begins to stop. It manages water, ammunition, pack animals, field workshops, replacement saddles and medical loads through a network designed to survive broken roads and separated columns. Moorish mobility exists because logistics has been taught to move the same way. A cavalry raid that outruns its supplies is a story; one that meets the next caravan exactly where planned becomes doctrine.
quote_en: “Mobility is logistics wearing a faster coat.”

role_en: Watch harbour approaches and carry warnings through waters too shallow for fleet escorts.
lore_en: A light clinker-and-carvel coastal hull carries one lateen sail, sweeps and a bow swivel gun. Local pilots use it to inspect shoals, identify unfamiliar shipping and relay signals between watch posts. Its low freeboard makes concealment easy along headlands, but limits open-ocean endurance and leaves it vulnerable once a frigate closes the range.
quote_en: “The harbour hears before the horizon answers.”

role_en: Intercept merchant traffic, close under lateen sail and overwhelm isolated decks by boarding.
lore_en: Salé’s corsair yards build long, narrow xebecs with three raked lateen masts and auxiliary sweeps. Swivel guns clear the target’s rails while grapnels and crowded fighting decks prepare the capture. The rig rewards skilled crews in changing coastal winds. Prize-taking drives the design; deep Atlantic swell and heavy broadside exchanges expose its light construction.
quote_en: “Bring the prize home with its cargo intact.”

role_en: Force sheltered harbour entrances and deliver concentrated boarding strength during a calm.
lore_en: A beaked wooden prow, a heavy bow gun and long banks of oars give this galley a fighting axis aimed straight at harbour chains and anchored ships. Lateen sails spare the rowers during passage, while protected waist platforms shelter the assault companies. Its strength depends on calm, enclosed water; rolling seas disrupt both the gun platform and the rowing rhythm.
quote_en: “At the chain, keep the oars moving.”

role_en: Protect Atlantic convoys with sustained cruising range and a dependable escort broadside.
lore_en: The polacre combines an economical cargo hull with square canvas forward and a lateen mizzen. Reinforced gun stations give it enough firepower to drive off light corsairs without sacrificing the water and stores needed for a long convoy passage. It follows merchant weather windows and conserves its crew. A dedicated fighting frigate can still out-sail it in pursuit.
quote_en: “Every sail behind us reaches the next port.”

role_en: Run down hostile privateers and maintain contact ahead of the Caliphate’s battle fleet.
lore_en: Shipwrights studying Castilian conventional frigates have lengthened the Moorish hull, cleaned its underwater lines and placed a disciplined battery on a single fighting deck. Maghrebi officers retain the aggressive approach of the corsair tradition, but prioritise rigging fire before boarding. The ship spends weight on speed and sail handling, leaving it poorly suited to a prolonged duel with a two-decker.
quote_en: “First take the wind. Then take the ship.”

role_en: Hold the battle line against conventional wooden warships and cover lighter boarding vessels.
lore_en: Thick oak framing supports two continuous gun decks beneath an ocean-going square rig. The Caliphate has adapted the bracing and ammunition routines observed aboard Castilian wooden vessels, pairing them with Maghrebi seamanship. These ships can challenge a conventional enemy line through disciplined fire. Their timber protection offers little answer to modern armoured capital ships or guns firing beyond their effective reach.
quote_en: “Let the little ships pass behind our guns.”

role_en: Anchor the main fleet and coordinate battle signals while sustaining the heaviest Moorish broadside.
lore_en: The Caliphate’s largest sailing hull carries three fighting decks, spacious signal platforms and additional damage-control stores. Broad beams and deep framing support its heavy cannon, while a carefully balanced rig keeps the flagship useful on Atlantic stations. Wealth and trained manpower are concentrated in every hull. Its deep draft restricts harbour access, and even this imposing wooden ship remains dependent on wind.
quote_en: “The fleet turns when our pennants rise.”

role_en: Bombard coastal forts and crowded anchorages from a surveyed position behind the escort screen.
lore_en: Two heavy mortars sit in timber beds tied into the keel structure, with the sailing rig shifted aft to clear their firing arcs. Moorish bombardment crews work from anchored stations and shore observations rather than chasing a target at sea. The compact hull can carry an unusually destructive siege load, but its open mortar wells and light defensive guns make protection by the fleet essential.
quote_en: “Measure the harbour before lighting the fuse.”

role_en: Carry soldiers, animals and siege stores between secure ports and prepared landing grounds.
lore_en: A broad wooden hull trades gun-deck space for ventilated troop berths, removable horse stalls and large stores hatches. A modest upper battery protects embarkation, while boats and derricks unload supplies after the escort secures the shore. The vessel gives the Caliphate sustained expeditionary reach. Overcrowding, bad weather and a contested landing can turn its valuable carrying capacity into a dangerous liability.
quote_en: “An army travels in the space below the sails.”

role_en: Advance under fire, open the way for shock units and hold the ground after the impact.
lore_en: Gao Fusiliers are proof that the restored empire learned the lesson of Tondibi rather than hiding from it. Their firearms are the ordinary foundation of Songhai’s new army, but their doctrine is more aggressive than a Castilian line regiment. Volleys are used to disturb and close distance, not to sustain an elegant exchange for its own sake. They expect cavalry, assault infantry or their own bayonets to finish the argument.
quote_en: “The gun opens the road. We still have to walk it.”

role_en: Maintain ranged pressure without powder, smoke or the logistical burden of firearms.
lore_en: The bow remains in Songhai service because modernity did not make silence, speed or independence useless. Sahel Bowmen can operate where powder is scarce, weather is troublesome or a musket report would reveal a patrol too early. Their rate of fire makes them valuable against light troops and exposed animals, while their simple supply needs suit frontier campaigns. They are not retained out of nostalgia but because some old tools still solve modern problems.
quote_en: “Not every storm needs thunder.”

role_en: Advance through firearm casualties without losing cohesion and break enemy gun lines at close range.
lore_en: The Oathguard turns national trauma into drill. Every member is taught the story of the empire that met Moroccan firearms at Tondibi and fell. Their answer is neither denial nor mysticism: they train until gunfire no longer governs their decisions. Oathguard still bleed and die like anyone else, but volleys that would shake ordinary infantry rarely stop their advance. They carry Songhai’s best firearms and wear the memory of Tondibi openly.
quote_en: “We no longer fear thunder.”

role_en: Enter breaches and disordered formations with heavy cutting weapons before the enemy can recover.
lore_en: Breakers are ordinary humans trained for extraordinary proximity. They carry heavy falx-like blades, axes and war machetes designed to convert momentum into a single murderous stroke. Their armour is lighter than that of the Oathguard because speed matters more than staying in a musket duel. Many future Sons of Tondibi are chosen from Breaker companies, but most Breakers remain mortal soldiers whose reputation comes from training rather than blessing.
quote_en: “One opening. One stroke. Keep moving.”

class_en: Mythic Shock Infantry · Miracle Vestigium Order
role_en: Cross firearm killing zones, shatter morale and turn a successful charge into immediate close-range slaughter.
lore_en: The Sons of Tondibi are a title, not a statement of sex; men and women who survive the rite inherit the same name. They wear layered desert ritual gear and carry Miracle-grade Vestigium falx or war-machetes whose edges burn red under momentum. Their patron’s covenant denies killing power to weapons it recognises as firearms. They are fearless and radiate terror in return. Yet the blessing does not make them invulnerable: entanglement, polearms, anti-Vestigium effects and battles that deny them momentum can still stop them.
quote_en: “Now thunder fears us.”

role_en: Anchor the battle line and protect firearms from cavalry or sudden shock attacks.
lore_en: Dendi Spearmen are deliberately uncomplicated. Long spears, compact shields and dense discipline give Songhai a cheap but reliable answer to cavalry and close assault. They are commonly placed beside Fusiliers or artillery where their presence allows more valuable troops to keep firing instead of breaking formation to defend themselves. They do not win wars through spectacle. They give the spectacular units somewhere safe to return to.
quote_en: “Stand long enough for the thunder to work.”

role_en: Scout, screen, pursue and appear on the flank before slower formations can react.
lore_en: Kurmina Horsemen form the everyday mobility of the restored empire. They are lighter than the Iron Riders and less dependent on specialised firearms than the Thunder Riders, which makes them easier to field across long campaigns. Bow, carbine and sabre combinations vary by troop. What remains constant is their purpose: find the enemy, hide Songhai’s true movement, then turn a retreat into a rout when the main blow lands.
quote_en: “See first. Turn first. Chase last.”

role_en: Break weakened infantry with a pistol volley followed immediately by a massed lance charge.
lore_en: Iron Riders are the image most foreigners associate with Songhai power. Rider and horse wear layered quilted protection reinforced where wealth allows with mail or metal plates. Their attack is built around one violent sequence: close under protection, fire pistols at short range, lower lances and strike before the target can recover. They are not European knights in desert colours. Their armour, horses and doctrine belong to the Sahel, adapted to a colder and more heavily armed age.
quote_en: “The shot makes the opening. The horse makes it permanent.”

role_en: Disrupt infantry and cavalry with mounted firearms, then charge or disengage before order returns.
lore_en: Thunder Riders represent the generation that grew up after Songhai decided firearms would never again be somebody else’s secret. Armed with carbines, pistols and sabres, they fight from the saddle rather than merely using horses for transport. A troop can harass, wheel, fire again or convert instantly into a close pursuit. They lack the crushing protection of Iron Riders, but their speed makes them the cavalry arm most comfortable living inside the enemy’s decision cycle.
quote_en: “We learned to make our own thunder.”

role_en: Strike caravan lines, remote posts and retreat routes beyond the easy reach of conventional cavalry.
lore_en: Camel Raiders extend Songhai power into the spaces between armies. They can move across long stretches where horses consume too much water or where a large supply train would announce itself from miles away. Their targets are rarely the strongest point of an enemy front. They burn stores, seize guides, cut messages and force commanders to protect routes that had seemed too empty to matter.
quote_en: “The road behind the army is still part of the battle.”

role_en: Protect the Askia and deliver a final reserve charge at the decisive point.
lore_en: The Askia Guard combines political prestige with battlefield purpose. Its riders receive the finest armour, horses and weapons the court can sustain, but their most important resource is discipline: they are not spent early. Kept close to the ruler or commanding general, the Guard exists for the moment when a line must be rescued, a breakthrough exploited or the safety of the throne itself becomes part of the battle.
quote_en: “The last horse moves when the throne decides.”

role_en: Mass gunpowder artillery against the point chosen for Songhai’s decisive attack.
lore_en: The Thunder Corps is the institutional answer to the weapon that once shattered the old empire. Songhai artillery doctrine favours concentration over technical extravagance: several reliable pieces placed where their fire can prepare one decisive assault. Crews drill for aggressive repositioning and rapid ammunition handling, but they do not possess Castilia’s industrial depth. Their pride comes from something simpler and more political: thunder is no longer arriving from the other side of the field.
quote_en: “The thunder belongs to us now.”

role_en: Maintain, inspect and prepare Vestigium weapons that ordinary armourers cannot safely service.
lore_en: The Forgemasters stand between workshop, archive and shrine. They repair damaged Vestigium housings, test unstable cores and prepare the Miracle-grade weapons reserved for the empire’s rarest formations. Their work is deliberately institutional: a sacred weapon that can only be understood by one genius is a liability Songhai has already learned to fear. Forgemasters travel with major armies in small detachments and are guarded as carefully as senior artillery officers.
quote_en: “A miracle still needs someone who knows where it cracks.”

role_en: Interpret divine pacts, maintain wards and define the ritual limits of blessed formations.
lore_en: The Diviners are not battlefield sorcerers throwing fire across the line. They are theologians, jurists and Vestigium specialists responsible for the dangerous border between language and supernatural law. When a blessing depends on what a god recognises as a firearm, someone must decide how new weapons, explosives and Vestigium systems fit that definition. Their rulings can determine whether a sacred defence functions at all, which makes doctrinal argument a matter of military survival.
quote_en: “A divine law is still a law. Someone must read it.”

role_en: Escort river columns, scout landing banks and suppress ambushes beside contested crossings.
lore_en: Sorko boatmen adapt the long Niger pirogue with raised timber gun mounts and light screens for the paddlers. A swivel gun in the bow covers an approach while spare paddles and shallow draft keep the boat useful among channels and sandbanks. Its crew reads the river better than any distant admiral. The narrow hull cannot carry heavy cannon or survive a sustained exchange with a coastal warship.
quote_en: “The crossing belongs to those who know the channel.”

role_en: Move grain, powder and replacement troops along the Niger between protected river depots.
lore_en: A broad, low-draft river hull carries sealed powder chests beneath a raised dry shelter, with sacks and water jars separated from the weapon stores. Poles, paddles and a simple removable sail let local crews work different stretches of the river. The barge supports Songhai’s land campaigns through volume and reliability. Seasonal shallows reduce its load, and the escort must secure the banks before it can unload.
quote_en: “The next battle begins with what we unload.”

role_en: Carry troops and stores between sheltered west-coast anchorages under escort.
lore_en: Songhai’s few sea-going transports use regional timber construction and practical sailing knowledge acquired through coastal trade. A stout hull, modest lateen rig and limited defensive battery protect the cargo without pretending to form a battle fleet. These vessels connect river supply to short maritime stages. They depend on pilots, sheltered ports and favourable weather; a major oceanic squadron can cut their route with little difficulty.
quote_en: “A useful ship carries the army one harbour farther.”

role_en: Hold forts, roads and frontier depots with shielded musket fire until the field army arrives.
lore_en: The Limitanei remain recognisably Late Roman even in 1717: crested helmets, oval shields, layered mail and heavy wool tunics still define their silhouette. What changed is the weapon in the other hand. Pyrobolarii companies carry rugged frontier muskets, wall guns and simple fire-rests designed for long service far from Ravenna. They are less refined than the Comitatenses but difficult to uproot from prepared ground, where shield cover, firing steps and old fortifications turn them into a stubborn first layer of imperial defence.
quote_en: “The frontier is old. The powder is not.”

class_en: Line Firearm Infantry · Field Army Core
role_en: Serve as the main Roman field infantry, combining firearms with Late Roman shield discipline.
lore_en: Comitatenses are the visual contradiction at the heart of Ravenna. They march beneath fifth-century standards in oval shields, ridge helmets and segmented layers of mail or lamellar, yet their primary weapon is a Roman-pattern flintlock musket. Spathae remain sidearms, not answers to a gun line. Their drill alternates protected firing ranks with shielded advances, preserving the cohesion of an ancient formation while delivering modern volleys. To foreign observers they look like history refusing to die, right up until the first coordinated discharge.
quote_en: “The formation survived. The weapon changed.”

class_en: Elite Firearm Infantry · Imperial Guard Line
role_en: Hold the imperial centre and deliver disciplined close-range volleys under extreme pressure.
lore_en: Palatini Sclopetarii are the elite firearm companies of the imperial field army. Their armour is richer, their weapons better maintained and their purple-red insignia unmistakably tied to Ravenna. Unlike ceremonial guards, they are expected to fight in the worst part of a battle. Their heavy muskets, reinforced shields and excellent drill allow them to absorb disruption that would fracture ordinary infantry. When the imperial standard moves forward, Sclopetarii are usually the men and women creating the space for it.
quote_en: “Where the purple stands, the line stands.”

role_en: Disrupt advancing formations with weighted darts, fire-pots and short-range firearms.
lore_en: The Plumbatarii preserve one of Rome’s oldest battlefield habits: hurt the enemy before the lines actually meet. Their traditional weighted darts have evolved into a family of incendiary, explosive and signal projectiles carried beside compact firearms. They are deployed ahead of the main line or behind shielded ranks, saturating approaches with smoke, sparks and sudden bursts before falling back into the formation. Their weapons look archaic until one lands among ammunition carts or a packed assault column.
quote_en: “The first wound should arrive before the first order.”

role_en: Pick apart officers, gunners and signalling teams beyond the main battle line.
lore_en: Ravenna kept the ancient title Sagittarii long after bows ceased to define the corps. Fulminis companies now carry long-barrelled rifles and carefully prepared ammunition, operating as marksmen around the flanks of the field army. Their clothing remains unmistakably Roman, but their tactics are modern: observation, selective fire and deliberate relocation after a shot. They exist to remove the small number of people whose absence can make a large formation hesitate.
quote_en: “Rome still calls them archers. The enemy knows better.”

role_en: Break armoured targets and fortified firing points with oversized hand-guns and wall pieces.
lore_en: Manuballistarii carry weapons too heavy for ordinary line service: long wall-guns, reinforced arquebus descendants and brutal large-bore pieces fired from hooks or rests. Their crews move in pairs, one carrying ammunition and supporting equipment while the gunner handles the weapon itself. They are slow, conspicuous and punishing to supply, but few infantry formations enjoy receiving their fire. Ravenna uses them where ordinary musketry cannot reliably punch through armour, barricades or monstrous hides.
quote_en: “If a musket cannot kill it, bring a heavier musket.”

role_en: Advance through hostile fire and deliver volleys from behind overlapping Roman shields.
lore_en: Testudinarii are the clearest proof that Ravenna modernised without abandoning its old body language. Broad oval shields overlap across the front while dedicated shooters fire through controlled gaps and over protected shoulders. The formation is not a literal ancient testudo marching unchanged across open ground; it is a seventeenth-century answer built from the same instinct. Testudinarii are slow and awkward on broken terrain, but terrifying in streets, breaches and narrow approaches where enemy fire has only one direction from which to come.
quote_en: “Let the century strike the shield first.”

role_en: Provide flexible firearm infantry for campaigning across Anatolia, Syria and the eastern marches.
lore_en: Sekban foederati are not dressed as Romans. They enter imperial service in recognisably eighteenth-century Anatolian clothing: long coats, wrapped sashes, practical headgear and locally favoured firearms, with Roman numerus badges added rather than replacing their identity. Ravenna values them because they already understand the terrain, roads and irregular warfare of the eastern provinces. Their loyalty is contractual, political and frequently pragmatic, which makes them exactly what foederati have always been.
quote_en: “Rome recruits the century it cannot become.”

role_en: Scout, ambush and contest mountain roads with long guns and local knowledge.
lore_en: Greek Armatoloi serve Ravenna because the empire understands that a mountain pass is better defended by people who grew up reading it. They wear eighteenth-century Greek and Balkan dress, carry long firearms, pistols and curved blades, and retain their own local leaders beneath Roman operational command. Their units are excellent at disappearing into villages, ridgelines and wooded slopes before reappearing on an enemy’s flank. The eagle on their badge is Roman; almost everything else remains proudly local.
quote_en: “The eagle may own the road. We own the mountain.”

role_en: Raid forests, villages and frontier corridors where formal Roman drill becomes cumbersome.
lore_en: Pandur foederati are drawn from the violent military borderlands of Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia and neighbouring regions. Their long muskets, dark coats, sabres and mixed personal equipment look nothing like Ravenna’s fifth-century core, which is precisely why the empire employs them. They excel in patrols, village fighting, forest ambushes and punitive raids where strict line formations lose their advantage. Roman officers rarely try to make them look Roman; a numbered badge, pay record and assigned standard are considered sufficient.
quote_en: “Rome counts them. It does not tame them.”

role_en: Hold cursed ground and sustain attacks where ordinary morale collapses.
lore_en: Cultores are soldiers of the imperial cult rather than robed civilians dragged from a temple. They wear simplified Roman military dress over ritual cords, votive plates and relic tokens, carrying muskets beside sacrificial knives and short spathae. Their sermons describe Rome itself as a living sacred continuity that must survive every emperor, plague and century. This faith makes them dangerously resistant to fear, but also easy for Ravenna’s priesthood to spend in places commanders would hesitate to send regular troops.
quote_en: “Rome is older than death. Prove you are worthy of it.”

role_en: Advance through pain and shock with bodies altered for close-range battlefield survival.
lore_en: Mutati were once ordinary legionaries, and Ravenna insists they still are. Their mutations vary: bone thickens beneath skin, armour fuses into scar tissue, additional eyes open under a helmet rim or a shield hand grows too large to release its grip. Many still carry firearms, though altered anatomy often forces customised stocks, triggers and harnesses. Their Roman drill survives in grotesque form. A Mutati cohort can look like a nightmare marching in perfect cadence, which is exactly why the empire deploys them where terror is useful.
quote_en: “The body changed. The number did not.”

role_en: Grind forward without fatigue, morale loss or concern for casualties.
lore_en: Revenant legionaries are the most literal expression of Ravenna’s refusal to release its soldiers. Dead troops are returned in damaged Late Roman kit, often with the same shields, muskets and unit marks they carried in life. Their firearm drill is slower than that of living Comitatenses, but terrifyingly consistent: a corpse does not flinch at counter-fire, hunger or cold. Officers use them for attritional advances, contaminated zones and positions where recovery of the unit is not expected. Even after death, the roster remains complete.
quote_en: “A discharge. A step. A discharge. A step. Forever.”

role_en: Protect imperial command and deliver pistol-supported reserve charges at decisive moments.
lore_en: The Scholae remain a courtly institution from another age, but their battlefield role is anything but ceremonial. Riders wear richly finished Late Roman armour over cold-weather layers, carrying carbines or paired pistols alongside long lances and spathae. They are held close to senior command, where their speed allows them to rescue a collapsing sector or exploit one already broken by infantry and artillery. Ravenna calls them ancient guardians; enemies experience them as disciplined heavy cavalry with modern firepower.
quote_en: “Old honour. New thunder.”

role_en: Screen armies, scout river valleys and chase broken enemies across the eastern marches.
lore_en: Vlach horsemen from Wallachia and Moldavia give Ravenna a cavalry arm built for distance rather than ceremony. They carry carbines, pistols, sabres and light lances according to local preference, riding in looser formations than the Scholae. Their duties are reconnaissance, screening, message interception and pursuit. In imperial records they are foederati cavalry. On the ground they remain men of the Danubian border whose speed lets Ravenna know what is happening days before a legion can arrive.
quote_en: “The Danube sends warning on horseback.”

role_en: Raid supply lines and fight fluid cavalry actions with carbines, pistols and sabres.
lore_en: Ruthenian Cossack foederati are among Ravenna’s most independent auxiliaries. Their mounted firearm tactics, steppe mobility and strong internal brotherhood make them useful wherever a rigid Roman column would be too slow. They attack convoys, screen river crossings and can dismount to deliver accurate carbine fire before remounting. Their allegiance depends on treaty, privilege and payment rather than cultural assimilation, an arrangement the Western Empire finds entirely familiar after thirteen centuries of hiring foreigners to defend Roman interests.
quote_en: “The treaty is Roman. The horse is ours.”

class_en: Roman Artillery Corps · Gunpowder Siege Support
role_en: Provide cannon, bombardment and Romanised siege fire for field armies and fortified fronts.
lore_en: The Ballistarii kept their ancient name while absorbing every useful form of artillery Ravenna encountered. Their parks now include cannon, heavy bombards, bolt-throwers strengthened by Vestigium components and incendiary siege engines descended from older Roman designs. Crews still organise around standards, numeri and ritualised commands that would look familiar to an officer from Late Antiquity. Only the thunder has changed. Ballistarii are less experimental than Castilian artillery, but brutally experienced at reducing walls and feeding long sieges.
quote_en: “The empire once threw stones. Now it throws thunder.”

role_en: Interpret omens, stabilise rituals and advise commanders on corrupted Vestigium phenomena.
lore_en: The Red Haruspices are where Roman religion, battlefield intelligence and Vestigium research become difficult to separate. They examine blood, organs, resonance patterns and captured relics with methods that appear ceremonial until their predictions begin matching battlefield events. Each detachment carries instruments, ritual blades, sealed tablets and a firearm for personal defence. They do not throw spells across the line. Their danger lies in telling an imperial commander when a place, corpse or relic can be exploited and when it is about to become something worse.
quote_en: “The gods are not silent. Most soldiers simply cannot read the report.”

role_en: Control mutated beasts used to break formations, hunt fugitives and clear fortified spaces.
lore_en: The Bestiarii descend from handlers, arena specialists and military animal keepers, but their modern kennels contain things no amphitheatre ever displayed. Mutated hounds, armoured boars, malformed cats and Vestigium-touched predators are bred or captured for specific battlefield tasks. Handlers wear reinforced Roman work gear, carry carbines, shock poles and restraint chains, and are trained to kill their own beasts if control fails. A Bestiarii detachment is less a single unit than a mobile cage full of bad decisions that Ravenna learned to weaponise.
quote_en: “The leash is part of the weapon.”

role_en: Break gates, crush dense infantry and turn a defended approach into panic.
lore_en: Colossi Mortis are not a natural species. They are assembled war-organisms built from enormous corpses, grafted armour, preserved muscle and Vestigium frameworks that allow the whole mass to move with obscene purpose. Roman plates and unit markings are bolted directly into flesh so even the monster remains administratively legible to Ravenna. Colossi are slow, difficult to transport and impossible to conceal, but concealment is not their function. They are released when the empire wants a wall, gate or formation to understand that conventional scale no longer applies.
quote_en: “Even the monster receives a number.”

role_en: Probe coastal approaches and maintain contact ahead of the imperial fleet.
lore_en: The imperial scout retains the narrow, low hull and continuous rowing gallery of a liburnian, enlarged to carry light cannon beneath a practical sailing rig. It can investigate coves and slip through calms while larger ships wait for wind. Rowers give tactical independence, but require space, water and food that restrict long deployments. Its guns warn and delay rather than settle a fleet engagement.
quote_en: “The eagle sees before the fleet arrives.”

role_en: Strike exposed wooden hulls and force enemy ships to break formation in confined water.
lore_en: A projecting bronze-sheathed ram is tied into heavy forward timbers, while enlarged oar galleries give the bow a brief, violent closing speed. Light bow cannon clear the approach before impact. The design depends on a favourable angle and a target unable to evade; a failed strike can tear its own framing or leave it trapped beside a superior battery. Admirals reserve it for sheltered water and disrupted lines.
quote_en: “One opening. One strike.”

role_en: Fasten alongside an immobilised enemy and turn the captured deck into an infantry battlefield.
lore_en: This broad galley carries hinged boarding bridges rather than the precarious single tower of its ancient predecessor. Grappling chains secure the target before shielded ramps lower from the waist. Cannon and protected fighting platforms support the crossing. The additional structure crowds the deck and raises weight above the waterline, making rough seas and accurate enemy artillery serious threats before the legionaries can engage.
quote_en: “Once the bridge falls, the sea becomes a road.”

role_en: Concentrate heavy forward fire against harbour defences and ships holding a narrow approach.
lore_en: The evolved quinquereme spreads its broad bow around a reinforced cannon platform, with oar galleries aft of the firing positions. Sail carries the hull between stations; coordinated rowing aligns the battery when the wind offers no useful bearing. Its forward weight and labour demands make it a specialised siege ship. Enemy vessels that reach its flanks can attack where its strongest guns cannot answer.
quote_en: “Bring the bow to bear.”

role_en: Drive ships from sheltered anchorages with a short-range incendiary projector.
lore_en: Protected tanks and hand-worked pressure equipment feed an incendiary siphon mounted in the bow. Heat shielding and separated stores reduce the danger without removing it. Oars hold the vessel on its approach while the fleet suppresses defenders. Wind direction, leakage and enemy fire can turn the weapon against its own crew, so imperial officers commit the dromon only when the attack path and withdrawal remain controlled.
quote_en: “Know the wind before opening the valve.”

role_en: Threaten packed anchorages and force defenders to cut their moorings under fleet fire.
lore_en: An expendable sailing hull carries combustible compartments, slow fuses and iron grapnels positioned to catch rigging. Its small crew steers the vessel until the escape boat can be released, then leaves the fire to finish the approach. The tactic exploits confusion and favourable wind rather than precision. A changed breeze, an early ignition or prompt enemy towing can waste the vessel before it reaches its target.
quote_en: “One hull buys an empty anchorage.”

class_en: Heavy Wooden Battle Ship · Imperial Line
role_en: Sustain the imperial broadside while lighter galleys attack the openings it creates.
lore_en: A deep wooden sailing hull incorporates Roman transverse framing, a pronounced beaked prow and protected waist galleries around two gun decks. Heavy cannon support ordinary line combat, while removable sweeps assist close harbour manoeuvres rather than propel the ship across oceans. The hybrid construction is strong but labour intensive. Its bulk and exposed galleries make fleet support essential against faster, long-range opponents.
quote_en: “Hold the line until the galleys enter.”

role_en: Coordinate imperial squadrons and sustain signals across dispersed coastal operations.
lore_en: The command ship combines an ocean-going rig with the high curved stern and open signal terraces of Roman naval tradition. Its protected chart rooms, spare rigging and dispatch boats support a fleet that mixes oared assault vessels with heavy sailing ships. A moderate battery preserves space for command work. The conspicuous stern advertises authority and presents an inviting target, while shallow ports remain beyond its deep keel.
quote_en: “Many prows. One command.”

role_en: Move legion detachments and siege equipment between imperial ports and secured beaches.
lore_en: The military oneraria develops the rounded Roman cargo hull into a capacious sailing transport with heavy loading beams and protected stores compartments. Oars and steering gear assist the final harbour approach, while a few cannon defend embarkation. Its practical strength is the number of troops and supplies delivered in one voyage. It cannot fight its way through a blockade and needs a secured landing before its crowded hold becomes useful.
quote_en: “The legion marches from the hatch.”

role_en: Form the disciplined mass of Napoleon’s field armies and shift rapidly between line, column and square.
lore_en: The Fusiliers are what make French superiority reproducible rather than ceremonial. Their blue-and-white uniforms, standard flintlocks and disciplined drill are deliberately conventional, because their strength lies in how quickly battalions can change formation and keep moving under fire. Officers are trained to preserve momentum rather than guard a perfect parade line. When elite cavalry and artillery create an opening, Fusiliers are the force that arrives in enough numbers to occupy it and keep the campaign moving.
quote_en: “The army wins because the line can move.”

role_en: Act as Napoleon’s veteran reserve, committed only when the battle demands troops that will not break.
lore_en: The Old Guard grenadiers are selected from veterans whose reputations were earned before their bearskins and gold distinctions were issued. They carry flintlock muskets, bayonets and sabres, but their real weapon is battlefield certainty: younger formations know the Guard is still behind them, and enemies know that France has not yet spent its final answer. Napoleon does not waste them on routine attacks. Their appearance usually means the battle has reached the moment he considers decisive.
quote_en: “If the Guard advances, the argument is over.”

role_en: Screen the main army, seize rough ground and harass officers and gun crews before the battle closes.
lore_en: Chasseurs fight in looser order than the Fusiliers, using cover, terrain and deliberate marksmanship to make the enemy deploy early. They are not independent romantic hunters; they are a formal part of Napoleon’s battlefield design. Their job is to blind, irritate and dislocate the opposing line so the heavier arms arrive against a formation already reacting instead of choosing. Long guns, compact packs and practical field dress make them recognisable as soldiers built to move before they are seen.
quote_en: “Make them turn before the Emperor arrives.”

role_en: Cross broken ground quickly, enter towns and breaches, and keep pressure on enemies between formal attacks.
lore_en: Voltigeurs are the light assault arm of the Grande Armée. They carry shorter firearms and reduced loads, trading some endurance in a prolonged line exchange for speed around obstacles and through dense terrain. In villages they climb walls, cross courtyards and appear through side streets before a heavier battalion could finish dressing its ranks. Napoleon uses them to keep an opponent unsettled between larger blows, preventing a damaged position from becoming orderly again.
quote_en: “A gap is useful only until the enemy closes it.”

role_en: Defeat armoured infantry and protected officers with powerful long firearms and hardened ammunition.
lore_en: The Carabiniers du Lys exist because France expects to fight enemies who trust armour. Their long firearms use reinforced locks and heavy steel-cored ammunition developed for penetration rather than volume of fire. Many wear breastplates or partial plate under dark blue coats, enough protection to remain steady while taking careful shots at difficult targets. They lack the speed of Chasseurs and the mass of Fusiliers, but when a Roman officer, Vestigium knight or shielded specialist must be removed at range, the fleur-de-lis marksmen are called forward.
quote_en: “Steel is only a question of calibre.”

role_en: Open roads, demolish obstacles and turn fortifications into entrances for the army behind them.
lore_en: French sappers carry the tools of construction and destruction in equal measure. Heavy axes, powder charges, pistols and reinforced work aprons give them a distinctive silhouette beneath bearskin or engineer headgear. They cut roads through frozen ground, prepare gun positions and destroy gates under fire. Their status is unusually prestigious because Napoleon treats movement as a weapon: a bridge raised in time or a wall breached five minutes earlier can matter more than another battalion standing idle.
quote_en: “Every wall contains a door. We decide where.”

role_en: Walk through conventional fire, break elite infantry and crush close combat with overwhelming protected force.
lore_en: France never accepted that the firearm had ended the knight. Gendarmes wear full-body Vestigium plate whose stored energy offsets enough weight to preserve shocking speed and mobility. Their armour can defeat ordinary shot, forcing enemies to aim for joints, use specialised ammunition or stop them at close range. Gendarmes answer with polehammers, warhammers and heavy maces designed to transmit force through armour. Pistols may be carried, but their purpose is simple: survive the killing ground, reach the line and make the line regret waiting.
quote_en: “Gunpowder did not kill the knight. It made him expensive.”

role_en: Lead sanctified assaults against positions where ordinary morale or ordinary steel is judged insufficient.
lore_en: The Knights of the Oriflamme preserve the oldest alliance between French aristocratic warfare and the sacred institutions of Napoleon’s empire. Their lighter plate carries relic housings, scripture plates and the colours of the sacred banner. Pistols and heavy polearms give them practical assault power, while discipline matters more than spectacle. They enter breaches where morale is failing, turning Church sanction and aristocratic prestige into battlefield momentum.
quote_en: “The banner enters first. Honour follows.”

role_en: Kill armoured infantry, elite officers and protected targets from behind French heavy formations.
lore_en: The Black Musketeers are among Holy France’s most feared firearm troops. Their dark wool uniforms and silver royal embroidery distinguish them from the Grande Armée, while long specialised flintlocks fire reinforced steel-cored ammunition developed to penetrate heavy armour. They are trained to work directly with Gendarmes: armoured knights absorb the dangerous approach, then lower or open the formation just long enough for a Black Musketeer volley to pass through. The combination turns French plate into mobile cover and French marksmanship into an execution line.
quote_en: “Iron wall. Black volley.”

role_en: Protect Napoleon and his command apparatus while remaining capable of immediate combat intervention.
lore_en: The Imperial Bodyguard combines the visual language of French nobility with the practical requirements of a modern headquarters guard. Partial plate, immaculate dark coats, pistols, carbines and fine swords allow them to fight mounted or on foot around the Emperor’s staff. They are not a supernatural order and are not intended to win wars alone. Their purpose is to ensure that the command structure Napoleon built does not collapse because a raider, assassin or sudden cavalry breakthrough reaches the wrong tent.
quote_en: “The Emperor commands the battle. We guard the ability to command.”

role_en: Move elite armour-piercing firepower quickly between threatened sectors without turning it into shock cavalry.
lore_en: Mounted Black Musketeers trade the long static firing line for speed. They ride to the point of crisis, dismount where possible and establish a compact killing position with carbines or shortened versions of the corps’ specialised firearms. Sabres and pistols are secondary tools, not invitations to cavalry duels. The formation exists because Napoleon values elite firepower most when it can appear somewhere the enemy did not expect it ten minutes earlier.
quote_en: “The black coat arrives before the warning.”

role_en: Deliver an armoured cavalry breakthrough against formations already fixed by French firepower.
lore_en: Mounted Gendarmes take France’s surviving knightly culture to its most extravagant battlefield conclusion. Rider and warhorse are protected by layered plate strengthened through Vestigium craft, while pistols and carbines supplement the lance and crushing sidearms. They are too costly to squander in repeated charges and too heavy for casual reconnaissance. Napoleon uses them as a decisive hammer once artillery and infantry have made an enemy formation hold still. The sight of polished armour accelerating through smoke is meant to break confidence before the lance arrives.
quote_en: “First the guns stop you. Then the horses decide the rest.”

role_en: Exploit weakened sectors with massed armoured cavalry that is more numerous than the Gendarme orders.
lore_en: The Saint-Lys Cuirassiers are France’s practical heavy cavalry. They wear polished cuirasses over dark blue coats rather than full knightly plate, carrying heavy cavalry swords, pistols and carbines. This makes them cheaper, faster and easier to field in large formations than mounted Gendarmes while preserving enough protection for a decisive charge. Napoleon uses them where artillery has shaken a line and infantry has fixed it in place. They are less legendary than knights, which is exactly why an army can afford enough of them to matter operationally.
quote_en: “Not every hammer must be a relic.”

role_en: Exploit openings, chase routed troops and attack exposed artillery or command elements.
lore_en: French lancers are built around reach and timing rather than armour. Their lighter horses keep pace with the fastest corps movements, while long lances let them punish infantry already disrupted by skirmishers, artillery or heavier cavalry. Pistols and sabres give them options once formation breaks down. They are rarely asked to create the first breach; their value lies in making sure an enemy who has begun to lose never gets the time to reorganise.
quote_en: “The breach belongs to whoever reaches it first.”

role_en: Deliver disciplined field bombardment and counter-battery fire in direct support of infantry formations.
lore_en: French foot artillery is less theatrical than the knightly arms and more important to Napoleon’s victories. Crews are trained to shift ammunition type, target and firing rhythm without waiting for elaborate ceremony. Batteries move with corps columns, prepare quickly and concentrate on the part of the enemy line that matters now rather than the part that looked important an hour earlier. Their guns are conventional enough to be repaired in numbers, but their employment is relentlessly deliberate.
quote_en: “The gun is ordinary. Where it fires from is not.”

role_en: Move artillery at cavalry pace, fire from unexpected positions and relocate before the enemy can answer.
lore_en: Horse artillery gives Napoleon a weapon that can change the geometry of a battle after it has already begun. Gunners ride with the battery instead of marching beside it, allowing pieces to appear on a flank, fire several rapid rounds and vanish before opposing guns complete their correction. Their uniforms are elegant, but the unit is built around speed rather than display. When French cavalry threatens one direction and horse artillery suddenly opens from another, the enemy often discovers that the real attack was neither.
quote_en: “The cannon arrives before the answer.”

role_en: Concentrate multiple batteries into a single overwhelming fire mission that creates Napoleon’s chosen breach.
lore_en: The Grande Batterie is not a unique cannon but a method of making many guns act as one weapon. Batteries share command, ammunition priorities and targets, concentrating fire on one section until formation, morale and command collapse together. Napoleon does not need every piece to be extraordinary. He needs enough ordinary guns solving the same problem before the enemy can move, reinforce or recover.
quote_en: “One hundred guns. One question.”

class_en: War Chaplains · Morale and Ritual Support
role_en: Maintain spiritual discipline, conduct battlefield rites and stabilise troops facing unnatural threats.
lore_en: French war chaplains accompany formations as part of the army rather than as ornamental clergy. A cuirass or reinforced coat beneath clerical garments protects them while reliquaries, field sacraments and records of the dead travel in the same kit as pistols and practical medical supplies. They do not cast battlefield miracles on command. Their value is psychological, institutional and ritual: soldiers facing revenants, corruption or catastrophic losses are less likely to dissolve when the Church has someone standing in the same mud beside them.
quote_en: “Faith is strongest when it shares the trench.”

role_en: Carry controlled sacred relics that strengthen French formations against corruption and supernatural pressure.
lore_en: The Reliquaires are custodians before they are fighters. Their armoured cases contain authenticated relics whose Vestigium effects are known well enough to deploy under strict ritual rules. Bearers wear ceremonial armour adapted for campaigning and carry sidearms for defence, but the object they protect matters more than the person carrying it. Used carefully, a Saint-Denis detachment can steady a formation under supernatural terror or suppress limited forms of corruption. Used carelessly, the relic becomes another unpredictable object on a battlefield already full of them.
quote_en: “A relic is not a miracle. It is a responsibility.”

role_en: Hunt corrupted elites, revenants and anomalous threats that conventional formations struggle to contain.
lore_en: Exorcist Knights are the Church’s answer to battlefields contaminated by things armour and ordinary musketry cannot reliably solve. They wear practical plate beneath white, blue and crimson religious markings, carrying blessed polearms or swords alongside specialised firearms and restraint tools. Training focuses on recognition, containment and coordinated killing rather than heroic duels. Their prestige comes from entering places where Gendarmes would merely survive and identifying what must actually be destroyed.
quote_en: “First name the blasphemy. Then kill the correct part.”

role_en: Lead the battle line and crush opposing capital ships with concentrated three-deck fire.
lore_en: Three continuous batteries sit inside a carefully balanced oak hull, with heavy guns carried low and lighter pieces above. French arsenals standardise spars, tackle and shot while preserving fine hull lines. This is the highest expression of wooden sailing warfare: powerful under disciplined crews, yet dependent on wind, deep anchorages and an immense supply of seasoned timber.
quote_en: “The wind carries the Crown.”

role_en: Hold the centre of a squadron while lighter line ships manoeuvre around it.
lore_en: A compact three-decker trades the Royal du Lys’s highest weight of shot for easier handling and a smaller supply train. Closely spaced frames support sustained broadside work, while carefully selected upper-deck guns restrain topweight. Admirals place it where the squadron must keep formation through changing wind, accepting that deep-water service still demands extensive dockyard support.
quote_en: “Keep the centre. Let the wings turn.”

role_en: Turn with the fleet and reinforce decisive sections of the battle line.
lore_en: Two well-proportioned gun decks give the Téméraire enough weight to stand in the line without burdening it with a third battery. Its broad lower hull and clean run aft reward skilled trimming. Repeated construction makes replacement spars and trained crews easier to find. It is France’s working battle ship, with fewer ceremonial fittings and more endurance than the great royal hulls.
quote_en: “Turn together. Strike together.”

role_en: Deliver exceptionally heavy lower-deck fire at the decisive crossing of enemy lines.
lore_en: Foudroyant carries fewer guns than the largest first-rates, but its lower battery uses heavier barrels and strengthened recoil beds. A wide waterline and generous stores steady the ship through repeated engagements. The design favours deliberate closing and accurate destructive fire; burdened batteries make shoal water and hasty changes of sail dangerous even with excellent French handling.
quote_en: “Let the first broadside decide.”

role_en: Direct dispersed squadrons and preserve command during prolonged fleet engagements.
lore_en: The flagship’s raised quarterdeck houses protected chart space, signal stores and a disciplined relay watch. Its rig is arranged to keep command pennants readable above gun smoke, while a strong two-deck battery allows it to remain with the fighting line. Experienced signal officers are its true expense: a magnificent stern cannot compensate for ambiguous orders or a severed mast.
quote_en: “Every sail must know the intention.”

role_en: Defeat enemy frigates and protect valuable convoys beyond the battle fleet.
lore_en: A long single-battery hull carries substantial guns above the waterline and provisions for extended independent service. Fine entry and careful weight distribution preserve speed without sacrificing an ocean-going structure. Captains can hunt raiders, escort stores or scout ahead of the line. The frigate’s strength remains relative: against a fresh two-decker, manoeuvre and distance become essential.
quote_en: “Bring the convoy home.”

role_en: Overtake raiders and maintain pressure on enemies escaping the fleet.
lore_en: Hirondelle gives up some battery weight for a long clean hull, lighter upperworks and carefully cut canvas. French crews practise rapid reefing and sail changes so speed survives uncertain weather. Pursuit captains aim to damage an enemy’s rig before boarding becomes necessary. Light structure and demanding spars reward constant inspection; a long chase can exhaust the ship before it exhausts its opponent.
quote_en: “The horizon is not an escape.”

role_en: Locate hostile squadrons and carry their position back to the fleet.
lore_en: The corvette combines a modest open battery with a weatherly three-masted rig and enough stores to remain beyond friendly sight. Spare spars and a practiced lookout watch matter more than broadside weight. It shadows superior ships at a safe distance, using sail handling to preserve contact. Damage to the rig can silence the fleet’s eyes far more quickly than losses among its few guns.
quote_en: “See first. Report clearly.”

role_en: Capture isolated merchant ships and disrupt enemy commercial routes.
lore_en: A compact square-rigged brig carries chase guns, prize supplies and boats intended for quick boarding. Licensed captains choose encounters by cargo value, wind and the chance of escape, bringing captured hulls into French ports. The rig needs fewer men than a frigate, but every prize crew weakens the original vessel. Profitable raiding therefore depends on judgement as much as aggression.
quote_en: “A prize is worth more afloat.”

role_en: Concentrate heavy direct fire against coastal works and defended landing points.
lore_en: The flat-bottomed pram spreads the weight of heavy guns across a broad timber platform. Short masts and working sweeps allow deliberate positioning in sheltered water; anchors absorb the demands of repeated firing. It supports assaults where line ships cannot approach safely. Low freeboard, poor ocean handling and limited speed keep it dependent on escorts and favourable coastal conditions.
quote_en: “Bring the battery to the shore.”

role_en: Lob explosive mortar shells over harbour walls and into protected anchorages.
lore_en: Deep reinforcement surrounds the mortar beds, while the main rig is set aft to clear their firing arcs. The ketch anchors under escort and uses surveyed ranges rather than an ordinary broadside duel. Shell stores demand strict separation from working fire and powder. Its value is the ability to reach behind a wall; exposed water and close enemy frigates remain serious threats.
quote_en: “The wall has a far side.”

role_en: Force crowded enemy anchorages to scatter before the French assault begins.
lore_en: An expendable sailing hull carries isolated ignition channels, combustible bundles and grapnels arranged for a final approach. A small volunteer crew steers under cover until its boat can escape. The weapon relies on wind, surprise and compressed anchorage space; a premature ignition or changing breeze can ruin the attempt. French admirals use it to open a harbour rather than count on a guaranteed burning prize.
quote_en: “One hull opens the harbour.”

role_en: Hold isolated sectors, manoeuvre without constant supervision and deliver disciplined flintlock volleys under pressure.
lore_en: Imperial line infantry are called ordinary only because every army requires a baseline. Recruitment, drill and promotion standards are severe enough that many foreign officers would classify an experienced Habsburg company as elite. Their charcoal-grey coats, black leather and double-eagle insignia hide few extravagances; quality is expressed through weapons kept in exact condition and soldiers expected to solve local problems without waiting for permission. When a captain falls, sergeants continue the plan. When supply is late, the position still holds.
quote_en: “If no order arrives, the duty remains.”

role_en: Take breaches, lead counterattacks and finish close battles that ordinary line companies cannot afford to prolong.
lore_en: The Double Eagle Grenadiers are veterans selected for nerve as much as strength. Their heavier kit includes grenades, reinforced coats or light cuirasses, stout muskets and short sabres for the moment a breach becomes hand-to-hand work. They are not berserkers. Their reputation comes from entering the worst part of a position with enough discipline to keep thinking while everyone else is reacting. A Grenadier battalion is rarely large, but its arrival tells nearby formations that someone has decided the ground must be recovered now.
quote_en: “The eagle goes where the line has already failed.”

role_en: Operate independently in forests and mountains to kill officers, scouts and key specialists before the main battle develops.
lore_en: Kaiserjäger are selected hunters, climbers and marksmen rather than decorated line infantry. Their rifles are individually maintained and often adjusted to the shooter, while field gear is deliberately sparse enough for several days of independent movement. They are trusted to interpret an objective instead of following a route step by step. In the northern forests, Alpine approaches and eastern marches, small Jäger parties can make an enemy column feel watched long before it sees the army that sent them.
quote_en: “One shot may save a regiment the march.”

role_en: Destroy armoured elites and dangerous medium monsters with powerful specialised rifles.
lore_en: Iron-Rifle Companies carry firearms too heavy and expensive for mass issue. Reinforced stocks, long barrels and hardened ammunition give them the penetration needed against Vestigium plate, mounted elites and creatures that shrug off ordinary musketry.
